source.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
source.authors: Adly Templeton; Tom Conerly; Jonathan Marcus; Jack Lindsey; Trenton Bricken; Brian K. Chen; Adam Pearce; Craig Citro; E. Ameisen; Andy Jones; Hoagy Cunningham; N. Turner; Callum McDougall; M. MacDiarmid; Alex Tamkin; Esin Durmus; Tristan Hume; Francesco Mosconi; C. D. Freeman; T. Sumers; E. Rees; Joshua Batson; Adam S. Jermyn; Shan Carter; Chris Olah; T. Henighan

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figures are not rendered in the web text; the relevant neuron-comparison findings are stated in the text.
record.tranche_reason: It examines whether neurons have interpretable, coherent activations using random samples and automated interpretability and specificity measures, rather than the original vision-neuron method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports direct results from inspecting random neurons and comparing their interpretability and specificity with SAE features. Feature-neuron correlations are not included as rows because that measurement does not itself report neuron polysemanticity. Results about SAE features’ specificity changing with activation strength are not rows for neuron-specific V7. Steering examples and results cited from other work are also excluded.
record.test_reason: Section 2.3 inspects random MLP neurons of Claude 3 Sonnet. Manually and with automated interpretability and specificity scores, it reports that neurons typically fire in multiple unrelated contexts. This bears directly on V2 (and on V6's claim that unrelated mixtures are rare). The method differs from the originals' feature visualization of vision neurons and SoLU layer-wise ratings, and the study is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAE features are rarely well correlated with individual neurons. Random MLP neurons are less interpretable and less specific than features and typically fire in multiple unrelated contexts. So dictionary learning finds features that inspecting neurons would not.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random samples of transformer MLP neurons and SAE features, with manual inspection and automated interpretability and specificity measures; it does not reproduce the original InceptionV1 neuron analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: For 82% of a random subset of 1M-SAE features, the most-correlated neuron in any preceding layer has Pearson correlation ≤0.3. Best-matching neurons showed almost no semantic resemblance to the features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable features found by dictionary learning in large LMs are largely not aligned with individual neurons. This is consistent with features being distributed across neurons, but it is not a direct measure of neuron polysemanticity.

record.problems: The neuron results are from one model. The model size is not reported. The paper provides qualitative or significance-only comparisons for these results, without effect sizes or stated uncertainty estimates; it also does not quantify the proportion of all neurons that are polysemantic.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant neuron-polysemanticity results omitted. The feature-neuron correlation result in Section 2.3 was left out because it does not directly measure neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Only one model is tested. There is no comparison across layers and no quantified share of polysemantic neurons.
Superposition is assumed as motivation, not tested as the cause of neuron polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization and noise are not examined as causes.
No comparison of activation functions, architectures or regularization.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined with better tools. Only random neurons are inspected by eye.
No analysis of neuron activation ranges or of scoring choices for neurons. The activation-range specificity results concern SAE features only.

missing.what: Numeric distributions of automated interpretability and specificity scores for neurons versus SAE features. Needed to quantify how uninterpretable neurons are; they are shown only in figures that are not rendered.

record.verdict_notes: The study is Scaling Monosemanticity (Templeton et al. 2024), not an original source. Model size is undisclosed. The neuron results are a small part of a paper focused on SAE features. r1 carries both the V2 support and the V6 challenge. r2 and r3 are comparative only.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and InceptionV1 neurons are not tested.
The study examines Claude 3 Sonnet only, not a range of language models or differences across transformer layers; it does not quantify the share of all neurons that are polysemantic.
The paper discusses superposition as a motivation, but does not test whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure or by packing more features than neurons.
Initialization, regularization, and training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure are not tested.
The study does not compare activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings, or test whether polysemanticity can be reduced without performance loss.

The study compares random neuron samples rather than specifically reexamining canonical neurons such as InceptionV1 4e:55, and does not establish whether any particular mixed activation pattern has a shared feature.
The paper does not test whether the classification of neurons as polysemantic changes across neuron activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Manually inspected visualizations for a random sample of neurons and SAE features.
rows.measure: Manual judgment of interpretability and activation contexts.
rows.baseline: SAE features in the random sample
rows.value: Neurons appeared significantly less interpretable than features and typically activated in multiple unrelated contexts.
rows.note: The paper reports the comparison qualitatively; it does not give a percentage of neurons with unrelated contexts.
rows.check: Polysemanticity is observed: neurons 'typically activating in multiple unrelated contexts.' For V6 this is the opposite of its claim that truly unrelated mixtures are rare. The judgement is qualitative only, with no share of neurons given and no layers stated.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Compared automated explanations and held-out activation predictions for randomly sampled SAE features and MLP neurons.

conditions.value: 100 randomly chosen features and 100 randomly chosen neurons

rows.measure: Automated interpretability, using Claude 3 Opus to explain features or neurons and predict held-out activations.
rows.value: Randomly chosen SAE features were significantly more interpretable on average than randomly chosen MLP neurons.
rows.note: The paper gives no effect size or numerical score for this comparison.
rows.check: This is a relative measure: neurons score lower on automated interpretability than SAE features. It does not itself show unrelated contexts or give a share of neurons, so it is indirect support for V2. Remove the V6 link, because lower interpretability does not show whether mixtures are unrelated or one shared feature. The neuron layer is not stated, and the scores sit only in figures that are not rendered.

rows.subject: Claude 3 Sonnet
rows.operation_detail: Scored specificity of randomly sampled neuron and SAE-feature activations using the stated automated rubric.

conditions.value: Random selection of SAE features and neurons

rows.measure: Specificity of the proposed interpretation for sampled activations.
rows.value: SAE feature activations were significantly more specific than activations of neurons in the previous layer.
rows.note: No effect size, sample count for this specificity comparison, or statistical test is stated.
rows.check: Neurons in the previous layer are less specific than SAE features. This is the same indirect, relative measure as r2, so remove the V6 link. No effect size or sample size is given.

relation.reason: Reports its own result on whether random MLP neurons are polysemantic.

tranche.reason: A different method aimed at the neuron question: manual inspection and automated scoring of random neurons against SAE features. Fits T2.

source_check.notes: All neuron findings are qualitative or relative to SAE features: no scores, shares, effect sizes, tests or layer breakdown. The paper is dated May 2024 (Transformer Circuits); arXiv v1 was posted 28 May 2026. It shares 6 authors with the originals. r1 carries one state ('observed') for both V2 and V6; for V6 that observation is the reverse of the version's claim, which the challenges verdict records.

statements.correction: Manual inspection: 50 random neurons and 50 random SAE features, layer not stated. Neurons appear significantly less interpretable and typically activate in multiple unrelated contexts. Automated interpretability (Claude 3 Opus explains and predicts held-out activations): 100 random features vs 100 random MLP neurons, layer not stated. Features are significantly more interpretable on average. Specificity (automated rubric): random features vs neurons in the previous layer, sample size not stated. Features are significantly more specific. No scores, effect sizes or tests are reported. Model size is not reported.
statements.problem: Three problems. (1) The text gives no layer for the 50-neuron manual inspection or the 100-neuron automated-interpretability sample. Only the specificity comparison names 'the previous layer'. (2) The statement puts specificity on the 100-vs-100 sample, but the text gives that sample size only for automated interpretability. No sample size is given for specificity. (3) 'Largest model in the pack' is not supported: the text withholds the model's size and calls it a 'medium-sized production model'.

statements.correction: The judgement that 50 random neurons typically fire in multiple unrelated contexts came from manual inspection. 100 random neurons were also scored with automated interpretability, and neurons in the previous layer with automated specificity. Both scores are only relative to SAE features. No per-neuron decomposition and no rate of unrelated mixtures is given.
statements.problem: 'Inspected by eye only' is literally wrong. Random neurons were also scored with Claude 3 Opus automated interpretability and with an automated specificity rubric. It is right that there was no per-neuron re-analysis with SAEs, transcoders or attribution clustering.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The inspected neurons typically activated in multiple unrelated contexts, and the neuron samples scored lower than SAE features on interpretability and specificity (r1–r3).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Rather than finding that sampled neurons generally resolve into coherent jobs, the paper reports unrelated activation contexts and lower interpretability and specificity than for SAE features (r1–r3).
